Concept.title: {=lXePKGIt}Martial Schools
Concept.text: {=9N832L1k}Dojos are neutral settlements where the player and AI can recruit students, purchase martial manuals that improve combat skills, join a specific school, or duel instructors for rank and reputation. Each dojo follows a distinct martial lineage. Improving relations with a dojo strengthens relations with all dojos of that lineage, and may improve standing with their sponsoring domain.

Concept.title: {=F1G2H3J4}Itto-ryu
Concept.text: {=K5L6M7N8}Itto-ryu is a prestigious family of kenjutsu schools emphasizing the principle of the 'one sword.' Practitioners, known as Itto-ryu kenshi, focus on decisive cuts, proper distancing, and timing. During the late Bakumatsu, its instructors were sought after by domains and samurai for dueling, military training, and personal defense.

Concept.title: {=P9Q0R1S2}Hokushin Itto-ryu
Concept.text: {=T3U4V5W6}Hokushin Itto-ryu is the northern branch of Itto-ryu, combining classical swordsmanship with battlefield practicality. Practitioners train in katana, wakizashi, and naginata, honing timing, distance, and decisive strikes. In the late Bakumatsu, the school supplied instructors to northern domain militias and duelists in Edo.

Concept.title: {=X7Y8Z9A0}Shinkage-ryu
Concept.text: {=B1C2D3E4}Shinkage-ryu is a transformative kenjutsu lineage that emphasizes strategy, posture, and subtlety. Practitioners wield katana and wakizashi, focusing on psychological control and precision. In the Bakumatsu period, Shinkage-ryu influenced many derivative schools, including Taisha-ryu, and trained elite duelists and samurai instructors.

Concept.title: {=F5G6H7I8}Jigen-ryu
Concept.text: {=J9K0L1M2}Jigen-ryu, originating in Satsuma, is known for ferocious, lightning-fast attacks with katana and odachi. Practitioners cultivate power, speed, and relentless offense. In the late Bakumatsu, Jigen-ryu kenshi were recognized for their role in domain defense and martial competitions, embodying the martial spirit of southern Japan.

Concept.title: {=N3O4P5Q6}Hozoin-ryu
Concept.text: {=R7S8T9U0}Hozoin-ryu specializes in spearmanship, particularly the cross-shaped jumonji-yari and naginata. Practitioners train in precise thrusts, fluid footwork, and battlefield awareness. By the Bakumatsu era, instructors trained domain militias and dueling students, maintaining a reputation for technical elegance and deadly efficiency.

Concept.title: {=V1W2X3Y4}Tanegashima-ryu
Concept.text: {=Z5A6B7C8}Tanegashima-ryu is a firearms school teaching the use of matchlock arquebuses. Practitioners learn coordinated volleys and battlefield deployment. In late Tokugawa Japan, Tanegashima-ryu instructors were vital in domain militias, bridging traditional martial culture and early modern warfare.

Concept.title: {=D9E0F1G2}Takashima-ryu
Concept.text: {=H3I4J5K6}Takashima-ryu teaches modern firearms techniques, emphasizing disciplined firing methods and unit coordination. Practitioners prepared for the changing nature of war during the Bakumatsu period, integrating Western rifles into traditional martial education for domain forces.

Concept.title: {=L7M8N9O0}Heki-ryu
Concept.text: {=P1Q2R3S4}Heki-ryu is a classical archery school, teaching yumi mastery for battlefield and ceremonial use. Practitioners develop accuracy, composure, and situational awareness. In the late Bakumatsu, Heki-ryu archers served both militarily and ceremonially, maintaining the prominence of mounted and foot archery traditions.

Concept.title: {=T5U6V7W8}Shinto Munen-ryu
Concept.text: {=X9Y0Z1A2}Shinto Munen-ryu is a kenjutsu school emphasizing adaptability, speed, and fluid techniques with katana and wakizashi. Practitioners were trained for dueling and skirmishes, preparing samurai and retainers for the unpredictable conflicts of the Bakumatsu era.

Concept.title: {=B3C4D5E6}Ogasawara-ryu
Concept.text: {=F7G8H9I0}Ogasawara-ryu is the classical school of mounted archery and etiquette, teaching yumi mastery on horseback. Practitioners develop poise, precision, and ceremonial bearing, serving as both martial and noble instructors in the late Tokugawa period.

Concept.title: {=J1K2L3M4}Hoki-ryu
Concept.text: {=N5O6P7Q8}Hoki-ryu is a kenjutsu school specializing in katana techniques. Practitioners cultivate strong cutting, timing, and defensive skills. During the Bakumatsu, Hoki-ryu instructors trained samurai and domain forces, ensuring readiness in duels and military engagements.

Concept.title: {=R9S0T1U2}Shingyoto-ryu
Concept.text: {=V3W4X5Y6}Shingyoto-ryu teaches a combination of katana, odachi, and naginata, focusing on versatility and battlefield adaptability. Practitioners excel in both dueling and larger engagements, sustaining their relevance through the late Bakumatsu period.

Concept.title: {=Z7A8B9C0}Oshima-ryu
Concept.text: {=D1E2F3G4}Oshima-ryu is a multi-weapon school specializing in yari, naginata, and variations such as jumonji and kagi yari. Practitioners develop complex thrusting and footwork techniques, serving as capable battlefield instructors during the late Tokugawa period.

Concept.title: {=H5I6J7K8}Tamiya-ryu
Concept.text: {=L9M0N1O2}Tamiya-ryu focuses on the long-hilted nagae katana, training practitioners in precise strikes and extended reach. The school's methods were valued for dueling and defensive combat by samurai in the late Bakumatsu era.

Concept.title: {=P3Q4R5S6}Moriuchi-ryu
Concept.text: {=T7U8V9W0}Moriuchi-ryu is a mounted martial school emphasizing yari and katana techniques. Practitioners develop coordination, balance, and tactical awareness for cavalry operations. In the Bakumatsu period, Moriuchi-ryu trained domain cavalry and retainers in practical combat skills.

Concept.title: {=X1Y2Z3A4}Owari Kan-ryu
Concept.text: {=B5C6D7E8}Owari Kan-ryu specializes in the sliding kuda-yari, offering innovative spear techniques. Practitioners train in precision, timing, and footwork. The school's unique weapons and methods were valued by Owari samurai for both ceremonial and battlefield purposes.

Concept.title: {=F9G0H1I2}Shinshin-ryu
Concept.text: {=J3K4L5M6}Shinshin-ryu is a kenjutsu school teaching katana and wakizashi techniques with an emphasis on timing and adaptability. Practitioners excel in duels and personal defense, maintaining a respected position among samurai in the late Bakumatsu.

Concept.title: {=N7O8P9Q0}Tatsumi-ryu
Concept.text: {=R1S2T3U4}Tatsumi-ryu is a comprehensive martial school training practitioners in katana, wakizashi, yari, naginata, and shuriken. The school's broad curriculum prepared samurai for dueling, battlefield, and self-defense during the Bakumatsu period.

Concept.title: {=V5W6X7Y8}Tennen Rishin-ryu
Concept.text: {=Z9A0B1C2}Tennen Rishin-ryu is a kenjutsu school focusing on katana, wakizashi, and occasional yari use. Practitioners were famously associated with the Shinsengumi, combining practical swordsmanship with rigorous discipline in the late Bakumatsu era.

Concept.title: {=D3E4F5G6}Nanbu-ryu
Concept.text: {=H7I8J9K0}Nanbu-ryu is a mounted martial school emphasizing bow and sword techniques. Practitioners develop horseback combat skills, coordination, and precision. In the Bakumatsu period, Nanbu-ryu kenshi served as cavalry instructors and domain retainers.

Concept.title: {=L1M2N3O4}Kyoshin Meiichi-ryu
Concept.text: {=P5Q6R7S8}Kyoshin Meiichi-ryu is a kenjutsu school emphasizing katana and wakizashi mastery. Practitioners cultivate precise cutting, timing, and fluid technique. In the Bakumatsu era, Kyoshin Meiichi-ryu trained loyalists and aspiring samurai in practical swordsmanship for both duels and domain service.

Concept.title: {=551Rfsop}Reforms
Concept.text: {=REFS21al}Change did not come to Japan all at once. From the opening of the country in 1853 to the Boshin War in 1868 and the Meiji period that followed, Japanese society underwent massive, but gradual, social, military, and economic reforms. Due to this, when the reform mechanic is enabled, not all troops are available from the start. Instead, better modern troops will gradually be unlocked over time either as the years pass or as the player's kingdom passes policies.

Concept.title: {=a3BLERbz}Keio Reforms (1865)
Concept.text: {=uzonvUWW}At the start of 1865, the Shogunate began a dedicated push to modernize their military. Beforehand, they had created the Sampeitai, or 'Three-Arms Corps', but that had been an unmitigated disaster. Prompted by the Kinmon Incident and Choshu's own civil war, the Shogunate's new reforms, forming units based on Samurai social rankings, ended in failure just as their previous ones had, but it started off the era of massive military reforms in Japan, which had been before isolated to a few small domains. These reforms unlock the Hoheitai and most of their equivalents, alongside units of unique organizations like the Mimawari-gumi and Shinsengumi.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Western Drill policy instead.

Concept.title: {=hEIiqFOl}Keio Reforms (1866)
Concept.text: {=sgDswQVO}In 1866, something thought unthinkable occurred: the Shogunate lost a war against Choshu. The Second Choshu Expedition had been intended to remind Japan of the Bakufu's strength, and to deal with the rebellious domain once and for all. Instead, the 150,000 strong army of the Shogunate was routed by the 4000 men of Choshu and their modern rifles, losing thousands of men and inflicting only a few hundred casualties in return. With this failure, and the ascension of Tokugawa Yoshinobu as Shogun, Japan entered a furor of reform. Yoshinobu himself worked to reform the Bakufu army, establishing the Hoheitai, Yugekitai, and Denshutai, while many other domains were incentivized to adopt proper modernized infantry.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are mostly unlocked with the Standard Uniforms policy instead.

Concept.title: {=LQZzQOJr}Meiji Reforms (1867)
Concept.text: {=tkAa93qw}Emperor Komei had opposed the entirety of the outside world, advocating fiercely for Sonno-joi. However, his son was not so inflexible. Following Komei's death of smallpox in early 1867, the teenaged emperor and his advisors began a series of reforms of their own, establishing the new Imperial guard, while other pro-Imperial forces, such as the Jinshotai of Tosa, began coalescing into a modern army of their own. At the same time, Choshu began reforming their remaining Shotai militias into proper units of their own, in preparation for the turmoil everone knew was coming.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Standard Uniforms or Officer Academies policies instead.

Concept.title: {=aEbjnf41}Boshin War Reforms (1868)
Concept.text: {=uKN9qS6E}Even as Japan reformed around them, many of the northernmost domains, as well as a few in Kansai, remained stagnant. The foolishness of this policy became apparent when the Boshin War broke out in early 1868, as the samurai of these domains suffered catastrophic defeats at the hands of peasants armed with modern rifles. These domains, most notable including Kubota on the Imperial side and Sendai on the Shogunate side, began to rapidly reorganize in an attempt to stave off defeat from those invading their domains.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Standard Uniforms or Western Drill policies instead.

Concept.title: {=9v5f6eq6}Shishin Taisei Reforms (1868)
Concept.text: {=BWWqeWJi}While in essence the same as the {BOSHIN_REFORMS_LINK} in their timing and reasoning, Aizu domain took a rather unique approach to reforming their military. Still unwilling to allow peasants in their military, Aizu instead implemented their 4 Gods Organization, classifying the samurai of their domain into one of four units, based on age. The Byakkotai were the youngest, made up of 16-17 year olds, followed by the Suzakutai (18-35), Seiryutai (36-49), and the Genbutai (50+), alongside a number of volunteer units that sprung up across the domain. Ultimately, however, these units were not enough to stave off the invasion of their domain and brutal siege of their castle.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Western Drill policy instead.

Concept.title: {=NeEiTkK6}Juei Reforms (1869)
Concept.text: {=CR3jonLR}Kishu domain, ruled by the Kishu Tokugawa, one of the Gosanke, or 'Three Noble Houses', of the Tokugawa Shogunate, reformed far later than most of Japan. Rather than taking inspiration from Britain or France like the rest of Japan, Kishu instead built their army along the Prussian model, implementing a conscript system that required a few years in active duty, then a few in the reserves, followed by service in the militia. However, these reforms occurred after the Boshin War, and ultimately came to naught as the Bakuhan system was dissolved and the private armies of the daimyo were folded into the new Imperial army.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Implement Conscription policy instead.

Concept.title: {=ON8mqnxs}Meiji Restoration Reforms (1870)
Concept.text: {=4iDrvn26}A small, final reform, this represents the units that were formed in the Meiji era, such as the Battotai or marines, that were added to the mod. While the time these units were created is somewhat outside the scope of the mod, and took place after these reforms actually happen, they were added into the game to fill their specific niches.{newline}{newline}If using policy based reforms, these troops are unlocked with the Implement Conscription policy instead.

Concept.title: {=lXePKasd}Social Castes
Concept.text: {=9NAB4L1k}The Caste Mechanic is an optional mechanic added in Bakumatsu to reflect the caste system of Edo period Japan. This caste system, put into place at the founding of the Tokugawa Shogunate, reflected the Tokugawa clan's deep paranoia and fear of being replaced. Due to this, it is often more of a restriction than a boon, and is not recommended if you want to enjoy a simple, easy playthrough.

Concept.title: {=IG1fHpiV}Kuge
Concept.text: {=vnNCl4Cz}The court noble caste, Kuge, or 'Ducal House', were in name the highest ranking caste and the rulers of Japan, from the capital of Kyoto. Mostly descended from the Imperial Family, the Kuge theoretically drafted laws and advised the Emperor. However, ever since the Heian era and later the short lived Kenmu Restoration prior to the Muromachi Era, the court nobles have been irrelevant in Japan. While they had a great deal of sway, and their words could be influential, they had no actual political power, and most court nobles instead made their living as tutors for the sons of wealthy merchants and high ranking samurai. Many would teach sons of the daimyo themselves. However, in the Bakumatsu they did regain some power as the emperor asserted himself, before being folded into the new nobility as the caste system was abolished.{newline}{newline}Pros:{newline}Right to command a personal retinue (+50% party size from clan tier and Steward){newline}Highly Influential (Earns an extra 2 influence daily){newline}{newline}Resistrictions: None

Concept.title: {=7cuzdfbI}Daimyo
Concept.text: {=wTxCBzId}The true rulers of Japan, the Daimyo were the mighty feudal lords of Japan. In the Edo period some 250 Daimyo houses existed, divvying up Japan among themselves. The poorest daimyo controlled at least 10,000 kokudaka of land, meaning that it produced roughly the equivalent of 1,500,000 kg of rice per year in goods, while the wealthiest was worth well over 1 million koku. The Daimyo themselves were subject solely to the Shogun, who could in theory revoke their land and titles at will, though the actual reality was somewhat different when it came to the largest daimyo. In practice, they were independent rulers, so long as they paid lip service to the Shogun and kept the peace. The player will automatically become a daimyo upon taking over or creating a kingdom.{newline}{newline}Pros:{newline}Leader of a kingdom{newline}Right to command a personal retinue (+50% party size from clan tier and Steward){newline}Highly Influential (Earns an extra 2 influence daily){newline}{newline}Resistrictions: None

Concept.title: {=01dc0ds8}Buke
Concept.text: {=Diyi7QGV}The warrior caste, Buke, or 'Warrior House', was the formal term applied to the samurai caste. In name, the samurai existed solely as warriors. However, in practice, by the late Edo period they were closer to a bureaucrat class, with most serving as domain officials. All samurai, except in Satsuma and Hitoyoshi domains, were required to live in their castle town, and required permission to even visit the villages. This was due to the Tokugawa Shogunate's paranoia, as they feared a rebellion or civil war that would unseat them. The samurai were themselves essentially split into two classes: high ranking samurai, such as the Shogunate's Hatamoto, consisted of families that earned more than 100 koku in stipends and served as ranking officials, and low ranking samurai, who served largely as guards and enforcers for their daimyo. By the Bakumatsu period, most low ranking and some high ranking samurai were broke, in debt, and struggling to make ends meet.{newline}{newline}Pros:{newline}Earns daily stipend based on clan tier{newline}Right to command a personal retinue (+50% party size from clan tier and Steward){newline}{newline}Resistrictions:{newline}Cannot engage in commerce (No workshops or caravans)

Concept.title: {=DoSReZx1}Hyakusho
Concept.text: {=PkLyT43W}The farmer caste, Hyakusho, or 'Hundred Surnames', was the formal term applied to the peasant caste. Making up some 80% of Japan's population at the time, Hyakusho lived in their own small, self-governing villages. They obeyed the Daimyo's decrees as required, but every village was in essence an autonomous entity, which governed itself, enforced its own laws, and only interacted with samurai as was required. While legally forbidden from using their own last names on official documents, Hyakusho clans not only had their own last names, passed down to all members of a household, but often 'head names', passed down to each leader of the household in turn. As such, it was not uncommon for a son, upon succeeding his father, to take up his father's name in turn while the father took on a new name in his retirement. Historically speaking, there was no legal difference between Hyakusho and {CHONIN_LINK}. However, their roles were so different that they were often considered two different classes by philosophers of the time, a split also used in the mod.{newline}{newline}Pros: None{newline}{newline}Resistrictions:{newline}Cannot command personal retinue (-33% party size from clan tier and Steward){newline}Cannot engage in commerce (No workshops or caravans){newline}Must pay agricultural tax (50% of all income from owned fiefs goes to kingdom leader instead of own clan){newline}Cannot enter keep of towns and castles unless a vassal of the owner kingdom

Concept.title: {=qun3E3A7}Chonin
Concept.text: {=0cg9FFOU}The merchant and artisan caste, Chonin, or 'Townsman', was the term applied to those of the peasant caste who lived in castle towns or cities. The Chonin were the core of the cultural flourishing in the Edo period, forming a wealthy middle class, to the point where the only people wealthier than them were the Daimyo themselves. Despite sumptuary laws enforced by the Shogunate, the Chonin were responsible for a trend of conspicuous consumption that led to ever more elaborate and refined artwork, literature, and theater, as well as the development of a form of proto-Capitalism, independent of the rest of the world. Nowhere were the Chonin more prominent then in the city of Edo itself, which had a population of some 600,000 Chonin, on top of 700,000 Samurai, making up roughly 1/28 of the entire popualtion of Japan at the time. Even so, the Chonin were highly restricted, as members of the peasant class, and were forced to always be below samurai. Historically speaking, there was no legal difference between {HYAKUSHO_LINK} and Chonin. However, their roles were so different that they were often considered two different classes by philosophers of the time, a split also used in the mod.{newline}{newline}Pros: None{newline}{newline}Resistrictions:{newline}Cannot command personal retinue (-33% party size from clan tier and Steward){newline}Cannot hold a fief as a vassal of a kingdom{newline}Cannot enter keep of towns and castles unless a vassal of the owner kingdom

Concept.title: {=4zs9V9yN}Eta-Hinin
Concept.text: {=C30bsAXr}At the very bottom of Edo society sat the outcastes. Often forced into these roles by hereditary profession, there were myriad different terms for these outcastes depending on which profession they descended from. But by far the most numerous were the Eta and the Hinin. Eta, a term meaning 'very polluted' or 'abundance of filth' applied to the descendants of leatherworkers, who were considered ritually impure due to their association with blood and death, while Hinin, meaning 'not human', applied to the descendants of mendicants and beggars. Despite their role on the fringes of society and the immense distaste that even peasants held towards them, these castes played vital roles in Edo society. Eta made all of the leather products used and worn in society, and took care of dead animals for nearby villages, making them often quite wealthy in the process, while Hinin acted as guards and policemen for the daimyo and managed the beggars and performers in an area, ensuring that only Hinin under their local organization could beg in each neighborhood, and only in the allotted ways.{newline}{newline}These lower castes built various complicated internal governing structures, most notable with Danzaemon in Kanto, a hereditary name passed down among a family of Eta who controlled all outcastes in the Kanto region. 13 men held the name of Danzaemon throughout the Edo period, and he was estimated to be worth roughly 50,000 kokudaka, making him the equivalent of a mid ranking Daimyo. Even so, the social stigma and discrimination against members of these castes was incredibly intense, to the point that aftereffects are felt even in the modern day, 160 years later.{newline}{newline}Pros: None{newline}{newline}Resistrictions:{newline}Cannot command personal retinue (-33% party size from clan tier and Steward){newline}Cannot hold a fief as a vassal of a kingdom{newline}Cannot enter keep of towns and castles unless a vassal of the owner kingdom{newline}Cannot engage in commerce (No workshops or caravans)

Concept.title: {=osiwP5oL}Gaikokujin
Concept.text: {=J84QToW3}Used in the late Edo period to refer to western foreigners, Gaikokujin were not a part of the caste system. However, after Japan was opened up, many of the restrictions upon them were forcibly lifted, and western tourists and merchants flooded the country. Many of the most successful of them, mainly arms dealers, gained a status comparable to that of the samurai, and were even given Japanese names and crests of their own.{newline}{newline}Pros: None{newline}{newline}Resistrictions: Cannot Play

Concept.title: {=pX2AJ9oC}Foreign Merchants
Concept.text: {=U37Ef6rB}To the merchants and businessmen of the outside world, the newly opened Japan was a goldmine. The price of gold and silver was cheaper than the rest of the world, and there was a huge market for outside products: most notably, firearms. Numerous arms dealers flocked to the archipelago, selling guns, uniforms, {FIELD_ARTILLERY_LINK}, and expertise in exchange for money and privileges. Found by walking around the keeps of any town, foreign merchants sell modern guns, artillery, and uniforms to the player. These wares each merchant offers differ by ethnicity. While all offer uniforms and antique flintlocks, British merchants offer the versatility of the many variants of the Enfield and Snider-Enfield rifles, alongside the best cannons, French merchants offer high quality rifles and cheap and light artillery, German merchants sell cheaper rifles, and American merchants sell all things repeating: revolvers, repeating rifles, and gatling guns.

Concept.title: {=1yyVKFnY}Field Artillery
Concept.text: {=FnYVK1yy}Cannons weren't just used to siege fortresses anymore in the 19th century. Every modern military would field a battery of artillery, and heavy guns were worth their weight in gold in Bakumatsu era Japan. Pieces of field artillery can be purchased from {FOREIGN_MERCHANTS_LINK}, but are very expensive and very heavy, meaning that too many cannons will bankrupt even an endgame player and slow the party's progress to a crawl. To use these pieces in battle, you must have artillerist troops, marked by a cannon icon on their unit. You can only have 1 artillerist for every 10 men in your army, and can deploy a number of pieces equal to half your artillerists. These guns also start in your reserves when you start a siege, and will not be lost even if the deployed versions are destroyed.{newline}{newline}Artillery can be deployed while pressing K during the deployment phase

Concept.title: {=Zt4XMACT}Special Ammunition
Concept.text: {=C66WEwA2}When using {FIELD_ARTILLERY_LINK}, each type of cannon has a default ammunition type, and a handful of special ammunition types. For example, the La Hitte Mountain Gun can shoot shells, round shot, or canister shot. For you or members of your party to be able to use specialized ammo in battle, the overall commander of your side in the battle must have the 'Stonecutters' or 'Siege Engineer' perk.{newline}{newline}You can switch ammo by hitting P before reloading the artillery in battle.
